findings.bug: Bounds guard uses 'vertexNum > getVertexCount()' so vertexNum == getVertexCount() passes the check, then vertices[2*vertexNum] reads one element past the end of the array.
findings.why_real: getVertexCount() returns localVertices.length/2, so a valid max index is count-1; the sibling setVertex correctly rejects with '> localVertices.length/2 - 1'. Passing vertexNum == count accesses vertices[length] which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
findings.how_to_prove: new Polygon(new float[]{0,0,1,0,0,1}).getVertex(3, new Vector2()) -> expected IllegalArgumentException 'vertex 3 doesn't exist', actual ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on vertices[6].

findings.bug: contains(node, identity=false) iterates the entire backing 'nodes' array (capacity length) instead of only the first 'size' elements, so it calls other.equals(node) on the null trailing slots.
findings.why_real: nodes is allocated to capacity and trailing entries beyond 'size' are null; every other size-bounded method (pop/down/equals/hashCode/toString) loops to 'size'. Calling null.equals(node) throws NullPointerException on valid input.
findings.how_to_prove: BinaryHeap h = new BinaryHeap(16,false); h.add(new BinaryHeap.Node(1)); h.contains(new BinaryHeap.Node(2), false) -> expected false, actual NullPointerException at nodes[1].equals(...).

findings.bug: Uses strict '>' and '<' for the containment test, so an identical rectangle (or any edge-touching sub-rectangle) is reported as NOT contained.
findings.why_real: Sibling overloads contains(float,float) (line 189) and contains(Circle) (line 201) use inclusive '<='/'>=' boundaries. A rectangle is geometrically contained in itself, so the inclusive semantics of the other overloads should apply; the strict comparison is inconsistent with them.
findings.how_to_prove: new Rectangle(0,0,10,10).contains(new Rectangle(0,0,10,10)) -> expected true, actual false (xmin>x is 0>0 == false).
